newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM would quit before yielding on strikes.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM would quit before yielding on strikes.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis was quoted on Thursday as saying he would rather quit than bow to demands from farmers and workers staging crippling blockades and strikes against his economic policies.
"I'd rather go home," Simitis told the monthly magazine Nitro when asked if he would yield to protesters to avoid falling from power.

"I am in politics to apply certain ideas about society," he said in a wide-ranging interview published on Thursday. "My job is to spread the existing money in a socially just way and that is why we must struggle not to succumb to blackmail."
The socialist prime minister was sending a clear message to strikers and farmers blockading the country's roads for 22 days, demanding higher subsidies, lower taxes and cheaper fuel.
On Thursday, the farmers marched on Athens to press for a meeting with Simitis, who adamantly refused to personally talk to them until they abandon their barricades.
True to his composed, mild-mannered image, he has opted not to use force to open up the roads but to wait out the blockade, which has seriously damaged the economy.

The tactic has shown some signs of success. Many barricades have been abandoned in northern and southern Greece. The farmers of the central Thessaly region have vowed to stay put and are spearheading Thursday's march in Athens.
Simitis has rejected all demands, saying Greece has no money to give and must catch up with its European Union partners.
In the interview Simitis said his vision of Greece in the next few years included a stabilised economy and an improved quality of life, with better public services.
He gave a pragmatic view of Greece's role in the Balkans and its relation with the United States and Europe, saying more work was needed to become a significant economic factor in the area.
"We need to get rid of the pirate attitude. We need to build for the long term," he said.
He said Washington was interested in ending Greek-Turkish disputes as part of its general policy but warned that Greece would not rush to agree to solutions contrary to its interests.
The polemical antics of his late mentor Andreas Papandreou, who delighted in antagonising Western allies, were a thing of the past, he said.
"We must get used to the fact that we need to talk. A constant contradiction towards everyone is a sign of weakness," he said.
Greece and Turkey have long been at odds over a series of issues, including territorial rights in the Aegean sea, the divided island of Cyprus and minority rights in both countries.
Days after Simitis took over from the ailing Papandreou in January, Greece and Turkey almost clashed over an uninhabited islet. War was averted with U.S. intervention.
